Growing Up Without Answers: Childhood in a World of Unspoken Truths.
Have you ever felt like childhood is a puzzle—one where the pieces never quite fit together? For one girl growing up in suburban Australia, that’s exactly how life felt. Her house was always full of noise and movement—siblings racing through the halls, a mother doing everything she could to keep the family afloat, and a grandmother whose hugs felt warm, but whose eyes held stories she never told.
Underneath all that day-to-day bustle, though, was a strange silence. It was almost like something important was always left unspoken. You could sense it in the air—moments when laughter faded, or when adults traded glances that said more than words ever could.
School brought its own mix of excitement and uncertainty. There were new things to learn, friends to make, and the usual playground dramas. But for this girl, there was also a constant feeling of not quite fitting in. Whenever someone asked about her background, the answers at home were always just a little too vague. Her family said they were Indian, but somehow, the details never quite lined up. She noticed how her mother and grandmother would get quiet, or change the subject entirely, whenever anyone got too close to the truth. It was as if part of their story was hidden away, maybe even too painful to touch.
Still, the family found comfort in their routines. There were shared meals around the kitchen table, bursts of laughter, and that simple joy of being together. But every so often, tension crept in—whispers behind closed doors, sudden silences, and that heavy feeling you get when adults are holding on to worries they won’t talk about. The grandmother, especially, seemed like she carried a world of secrets behind her soft smile. She was loving, always there with a gentle touch, but there was a sadness she never explained.
As the girl got older, she started seeing the differences more clearly. Neighbors sometimes kept their distance. Strangers would stare just a little too long. Her family’s skin was a bit darker than most of the people around them, and even though no one said it out loud, it was something everyone noticed. She could tell that her family’s story wasn’t like her classmates’. But every time she tried to ask about it, the conversation would just slip away, replaced by uncomfortable silence.
Her mother was always working—juggling jobs, hustling to make sure her kids had what they needed. She was strong and practical, but when it came to her own past, she’d never share much. Just a sentence or two, then she’d change the topic. The grandmother was the same—her stories about the past were always carefully edited, with certain names and places left out, like pieces of a puzzle that had gone missing.
Even with all that silence, the girl’s curiosity only grew. She watched her friends talk about their family histories, their traditions, the places they came from. And she wanted that too—the certainty, the sense of belonging. But at home, the past was a closed door, and nobody seemed willing to open it.
Over time, it became clear this wasn’t just about privacy—it was about protection. The family’s silence was a shield, a way to keep themselves safe in a world that could be unkind to anyone who stood out. There was a real fear there—fear of being judged, of being treated differently, of losing what little security they’d managed to build.
So as the years went by, the questions only got louder in her heart. Who am I, really? Where did I come from? And why do we feel the need to hide? That search for answers became something she couldn’t let go—a quiet obsession that would shape her life. Even as the world outside kept changing, her family’s secrets stayed locked away, just waiting for the right moment to finally come out.
